utterances.text: When we are informed in a timely manner like this, we wouldn't have any objections, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is -- like this, you consider this a timely. Does that mean that you do not oppose, Mr. Lukic? I'm trying to fully understand your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't by heart if all the deadlines are respected like 92 ter 30-day deadline. But if it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll further hear from you whether it meets any opposition or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Selak. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that 65 ter 08797 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, just prior to the break we were talking about military notebooks in general, and I want to now ask you one more general question, then some specific questions about your practice, your notebooks. First, was there an obligation once a military notebook was completed, was filled, that it be turned in?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you left the military service, did you turn in your last notebook?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see on the screens before us a notebook. Do you recognise this book, or the page that we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. That is my notebook. And the date is the 9th of -- 19th of December, 1991. That is when I started using that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the book that you used until the time that you left military service?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without taking -- without going to your brief-case, did you bring the original with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Should the Chamber, Mr. Mladic, or his attorneys wish to view the original, are you willing to make it available for them to look at?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my intention now to look at a excerpt of the book, the pages that are directly relevant to the meetings today. It's not beyond all possibility that some point later in the trial the Chamber may wish to -- or the Prosecution or the Defence may wish to tender another entry from the book, so I'll be guided by the Chamber whether it would prefer that I seek to mark it for identification now or to leave it as is and simply tender the pages. I do want the foundation that has just been laid to be connected to the book should it ever be needed or other excerpts be needed in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber accepts that you use only an excerpt at this moment. However, if later on portions should be added to it, because we then will have to decide whether we make new exhibit numbers or whether we include them with the -- with leave of the Chamber in the existing ones, it is important that you refer to dates primarily, and to -- if there are page numbers, not exceptionally not the e-court page numbers but the page numbers of the notebook itself. And there I already see a possible first problem. Because on my English version on the first page I see a number 1 at the bottom of the page; whereas, in the original, I do not see -- not see a corresponding number 1. But for the time being, we can proceed as you suggest. But dates are, at this moment, most important, and perhaps you could also use ERN numbers which are found in the original so that it's easier to retrieve pages at a later stage in this original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And with respect to the concern that the Chamber raised earlier with respect to another large document, I would note that this book has been tendered and admitted into evidence in its entirety in several other cases, so the Chamber would be able -- would have the means to confirm that the original 65 ter number hasn't -- hasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I -- yes. But I take it that the pages you're going to use, that they -- you're tendering those as part of this -- today's excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have a subsidiary derivative exhibit, Your Honour. The same 65 ter number but with the letter A, and it is simply the meeting notes from the two meetings that have been discussed here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed as suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, yesterday did I ask you to identify the pages in your notebook which contained your contemporaneous meetings of the two meetings which you've given evidence about today, the one related to Kozarac and the one related to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that we have on our screens 08797A. These are pages taken -- or a selection of four pages taken from Mr. Selak's notebook. They are pages 117, 118, 124, and 125 of the original e-court pages; and e-court pages 150, 151, 158, and 159 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Selak, we can see one of the pages before us. We can zoom in to either side if that assists. But can you tell us which meeting this particular entry refers to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, the other one. Yes, yes, this is it. That's the meeting at the commander's, the commander of the 5th Krajina Corps. I attended the meeting and I jotted down the questions that were dealt with at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the meeting in which Kozarac was discussed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it here, the third question dealt with: "In Kozarac, because of a roadblock," alleged roadblock, "800 dead, 1200 captured." Your Honours, this is the 343rd Motorised Brigade that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct - and so that we mark it clearly for the record - that your note on this meeting begins on the internally numbered page of your notebook, page number 223.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. 223, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we advance to the next page and look at 224. And this is the internal number on the notebook itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this also contain some notes --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we advance to e-court page 3 of 08797A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we cannot verify the number at the top of the page because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please return to it, to the page that -- the second page, and focus on the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we now please advance to the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you guide us to where the -- the text or your notes about -- that are relevant to your evidence begin. On the left-hand page or the right-hand page? And then we'll zoom in.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, there is the total number of personnel in the corps and other attached units, so it's about one hundred one thousand men. So on the 1st of June in terms of the food that had to be provided by the logistics base, that was the personnel level of the 1st Krajina Corps and its subordinated units in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak can you guide us to where your notes about the meeting in which Manjaca was discussed? Can you guide us to where your notes on that meeting begin?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It's not on this page. No, not Manjaca. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. We'll have to look further on. Manjaca is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please advance to the next page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. 997. Your page 997. Page -- or, rather, bullet point 4. These are the orders of the corps commander, the 4th task, the fourth point is that POW camp at Manjaca should urgently be established for approximately 2.500 persons. Urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to the internal numbering of the notebook it is page 238, and according to the evidence stamp of the Office of the Prosecutor that number ends in 6997. Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders these pages 65 ter 0797A [sic] as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 08797A will be Exhibit P253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, the Chamber over the course of the last few weeks has received evidence describing Manjaca and the conditions there. Did you ever personally visit Manjaca while it was being used to detain prisoners? After this order was given.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit the camp at Manjaca. May I give a boarder explanation, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you to listen to the questions carefully and answer them. Mr. Groome is limited in his time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can ask you, and this is my last question for you here today, is can you describe for the Chamber what you observed when you went and visited Manjaca? And if you could begin telling us when precisely it was that you visited the camp.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, the second day after this meeting, the assistant corps commander for logistics, Colonel Vaso Tepsic and I took one car and General Talic, the corps commander, took another car and we went to Manjaca together. General Talic went to see the commander of the training grounds up there, Colonel Popovic, and Colonel Tepsic and I went to the former stables. I mean, that's where stables, barns were for cattle, and now they were used for putting up prisoners of war. Colonel Tepsic and I entered these buildings, and we found about 100 to 130 men there. Some of them had been beaten up. You could see blood on their faces and on their clothing. Some of them were naked to the waist. They were working on cleaning the barns of the waste, the cattle waste that had remained. That's how they were put up there. The officer who was on duty issued an order to them that said, Attention. None of them moved. They all lowered their heads. It was terrible. I mean, the very -- the very image that I saw then, I tell you, it sends shivers down my spine to this day. Then we went to Colonel Popovic. However, he said that he would take other measures. Unfortunately, quite a few people were killed in this camp. First they were beaten up, and later on they succumbed to the wounds due to their mistreatment. However, there are records - I don't have them personally, but there are records of the names and surnames of the persons who were mistreated and thereby killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, earlier today at transcript page 34 you said that the Manjaca complex was approximately 700 hectares. My question to you is: Are you able to estimate how much of this 700 hectares was reserved for the detention of prisoners? What part of it was used to keep these people detained?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I personally think that there were six or seven buildings there, prefabricated buildings that were used as cattle barns before. So the area is perhaps a hectare and a half or two, because there was free space among the buildings. I never actually measured it. But it seems to be, say, one and a half hectares or two. It was to the left of the main road that led to these training grounds, and on the right-hand side there were proper buildings for the command, headquarters, for soldiers manning the training grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Since we have dealt with your diary, could I take you back to the excerpt, the four pages under the number A. And could I have a look at the second page in English. Mr. Selak, I think we have it here. One second, please. Yes. Could we zoom in under upper half of the ... This is the last part of your report on a meeting with the 5th Corps commander on the 27th of May. The last line reads: "He is against the war option, 800 killed." Could you tell me who is the "he" in this sentence and what does this actually mean? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this last question where it says "he is against the war option" and then he is surprised by the fact that 800 persons were killed, he was afraid because it was international law of war that had been violated. These were civilians. The population of Kozarac. And that is why his order was to report that 80 persons were casualties there. Even that is too much. Somebody should have been held responsibility. However, he was afraid that this information would reach the command of the army and that he would be held responsible as the superior officer because he had not taken measures against the perpetrator of this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make sure that I do understand it. Is this General Talic, then, "he," or is it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These are bullet points. And the corps commander spoke about this at this meeting. So if you look at this other one that has to do with the Chief of Staff, Main Staff, analyse the food rations for the troops of the 5th Corps and others, so he is issuing orders to have this analyses carried out. All of these are orders of the commander of the 5th Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, to fully understand this line, if you say, He is again the war option, that is ambiguous language. It could mean that he is against --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The corps commander, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wait for one second. It could mean that he is against going to war or continue the war, because, already, 800 people have been killed. It could also be that you say he is against the war option, he is against reporting it as a war event, those 800 killed. Could you elaborate a little bit more about what now exactly it means that he is against the war option? Is that part -- is that related to the reporting on the events, or is it related to what General Talic would like to happen in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I understand the question. I personally knew General Talic very well. Basically he was not a bad man. However, he carried out -- he had to carry out the orders of his superior command. He was carrying out orders. I also think that he was not pleased by this number of citizens who had lost their lives. He had to report about that, but he had to take disciplinary measures against the perpetrators and that's the commander of the 343rd Command Motorised Brigade in Prijedor. However, no measures were taken, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, that commander, later on, received the rank of colonel. But Talic was carrying out orders of his superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let me verify whether I understood your answer. Is it that General Talic expressed that he was not happy with the conflict to be resolved by armed force and referred to the 800 people already killed and that he would prefer another option than armed force. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. General Talic officially stated that, that he was not in favour of the war option. However, the corps did exist and he carried out -- he implemented the policy of the government of Republika Srpska. He had to do that because he was their organ. I personally think that General Talic was not in favour of that war option. In this area where Muslims were a majority population, there were well known operations carried out even during the Second World War. Unfortunately, many people lost their lives then as well. I don't know about the future, what it's going to be like either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic and you'll find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Selak.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: His Honour has already introduced me, so can we start now?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you say that information was being concealed when we speak about these 80, 800 casualties in Kozarac. In your view, the duty was to report that 800 persons had been killed.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the report said that 80 persons had been killed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of what had been reported --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we now have a document in e-court now. 070 -- or, rather, 07128. The number assigned to it was P247.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document says that these persons were killed in combat; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is not stated that they had been liquidated. So this is the document that went to the superior command; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. However this document -- actually, this is a report. It is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've already heard that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: This is false information being sent to the superior command precisely because they were afraid of what the consequences would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak please answer the questions put by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is interested in a matter which is different than the matter; that is, about reporting and what information was received at the higher levels. That's what Mr. Lukic is concerned. And you have already explained extensively that what was reported was not in accordance with the truth. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what sort of information reached the 1st Krajina Corps? Do you know whether misinformation arrived from the field? Were the reports correct? Do you have any information about whether there were reports about who was killed by whom and when? Do you have any -- did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Sir, at the briefing when Colonel Marcetic was there, he received information from the commander of the 343rd Motorised Brigade from Prijedor. Information about what had happened that day, how many people were killed. The brigade command reported and Martic -- Marcetic informed the commander of what had happened, and then later reports were sent to the command of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will pause so that everything can be transcribed. It doesn't mean that I'm not happy with your answer. Are you familiar with any cases when no reports were compiled in the field?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the reports were not correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, May, June, July, at the beginning of the conflict, were communications interrupted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Communication lines were cut off but there were couriers, and the units had to use such couriers. Similarly my unit, because that was a wider area of responsibility. So couriers were used to communicate information and to forward reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 49 today, you said that you were at this collegium with General Talic, this meeting. In the document that you provided us with today, P253, is the number assigned to it -- no, that's a mistake. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P249.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document that consists of two maps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And two charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. Could we zoom in and see the top part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that this was the situation after the 18th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This chart depicts the 1st Krajina Corps structure. But you're not included there.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of the 1st Krajina Corps. I was not included there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 4 now, please. Here, in the middle of this chart we can see that you were subordinated to Major-General Djukic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How is it that you were present at that collegium, at that meeting of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I've explained this previously. As commander of the logistics base, I was always available to the corps commander, and he would contact me by phone and tell me when there were meetings that I could be present in order for me to obtain information so that my organs could react more expeditiously. This was to speed up things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you received an invitation to attend.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That wasn't a regular thing. You didn't have to attend unless you were invited?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't have to but there was no reason. If I was invited, there was something important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant if they don't call you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, if they didn't invite me, no, it was not my duty to attend in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were responsible for supplying the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Not only the 1st Krajina Corps, but all the units in the area of responsibility in the territory that was depicted here a little earlier on. There was the Military Technical Academy, there was the rocket brigade under the army's command, the communication centre, so the logistics base supplied all the units that were present in that area. The logistics base in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These diagrams, these charts, in fact, mention who is from Serbia and who from Bosnia-Herzegovina. From among the people of the Serbian -- of Serbian ethnicity. In terms of percentages, how many people were there Serbia in the VRS? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In terms of percentages, I couldn't say. But, Your Honours, when the VRS was established on the 18th of May, I was in Banja Luka. Not a single officer or junior officer from Serbia, Montenegro, or -- didn't leave their duties in the corps command, in the rocket brigade, apart from those who were due to retire. I don't know about the percentages, but not a single officer left apart from those who retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the situation in lower units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: When I'm talking about the corps, that also includes its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your testimony today is that the entire command structure of brigades and battalions remained the same?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Apart from the soldiers who were performing their military service, who weren't from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They could go to their homes, to Macedonia, to Montenegro, to Serbia, and so on and so forth, but all the officers who remained on the payroll. In my notebook, an entry was made when someone said that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would continue paying salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any people from Serbia in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: People from Sandzak, Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I believe that that was the case, but I do not have any information. I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, could you please make a short pause between question and answer, and Mr. Lukic will do the same so that the interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have heard of Sefer Halilovic. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He's from Serbia, Sandzak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The soldiers from the 1st Krajina Corps were from the territory that was covered by the 1st Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The soldiers performing their military service were not only from that territory but from wider areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about people who were members of the 1st Krajina Corps, about the men who were members from 1992 onwards, ordinary soldiers. Is it correct that 99 per cent of them were from the territory of Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There was an officially mobilisation carried out in that area, and all those fit for military service, they'd already been given war-time assignments. They had to respond to the mobilisation and go to their units. That was the case in my logistics base. Disciplinary measures, judicial measures were taken against those who failed to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that anyone who responded to the mobilisation would be assigned to a unit and issued with a weapon and a uniform?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. There was a training, but the soldier couldn't immediately receive a weapon without training. First it was necessary to be trained and then weapons would be issued. They would be given a uniform, yes, but weapons only having completed the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Members of the reserve force immediately received weapons and uniforms because they had already received training.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. But there were no more reserves after the mobilisation. There were no more reservists apart from the officers and soldiers performing their military service, but they would have been members of those units. There was only an age difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would also agree with me that members of the Muslim and Croatian ethnic groups did not largely respond to the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. But there were also threats that were issued. I have a document here, too, Your Honours, where it says that the Crisis Staff requested that members of the Croatian and Muslim ethnicity be removed from Serbian units because they were not trusted. I do have such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I do apologise. When you speak about the mobilisation, are we talking about September 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time were any threats issued or did people not respond, the Muslims and the Croats, because they didn't want to go to war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: There were such cases in my unit that had about two and a half thousand men. I think there were several who did not respond. I don't know why. Was it because it was a matter of logistics or not? But politics was involved, Your Honours. And men did go to Croatia to fight in the war and to border areas in the direction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so there were political problems with regard to this matter. But I can't really go into details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 2003 in the Brdjanin case, you said, line 11 to line 14, that the Bosniaks did not respond to the mobilisation to join war-time, or, rather, combat units that were supposed to go to Croatia. Because of that, the Bosniaks were not trusted. Would you stand by what you stated there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Similarly, at page 12928 in the same case, you said all the mobilised units were mobilised in accordance with the law. They received weapons from war depots. That's how it was translated. Would you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, in accordance with instructions from the Assembly of Yugoslavia from 1990 to 1991, Territorial Defence units had to be disbanded and their weapons had to be returned to JNA depots, or, rather, to logistics bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will deal with that later, but I'm asking you about the units mobilised in 1991 and the units mobilised at the beginning of 1992. Were they legally mobilised at the time in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: In my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at the time were they issued with weapons in a lawful manner?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us which military depots for weapons and equipment remained in the territory of Republika Srpska and which remained in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I can speak about the logistics base in Banja Luka, and everything remained in the territory of Republika Srpska in one depot there. The Sarajevo base, Sarajevo Logistics Base, had a depot in the area of Han Pijesak. In some cases, equipment was left there. In others, that wasn't the case. But in the logistics base in Banja Luka it was handed over to Republika Srpska to the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't have information for the area covered by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, I have no information. I wasn't a member of that formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the Muslims joined the police to a larger extent, and this is how they obtained weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I am not aware of that. I'm not aware of them joining the police force. I don't think that's -- well, in fact, that information wasn't made public. I know nothing about that. So I was a bit surprised by this question. I never heard of anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you say you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor municipality, the head of the Territorial Defence was Mr. Mundjinen [phoen]. Did you know that? Did you co-operate with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I did not co-operate with him. I heard of him. I did not co-operate with him. There was no need for him to co-operate with me or vice versa. I never met up with him. Or at least I don't remember that I -- I ever saw him. I heard of him, but that's all. The name does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On page 12951 also in the Brdjanin case, on the 15th of January, 2003, you testified about volunteer units and you said they were connected to the respective parties and that they carried out party tasks. Would you say the same today?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. Voluntary units were paramilitary units which were set up by the respective parties as well as the regional staffs. I know about Bosnian Krajina but that applied to the entire Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's how they were set up and they were armed by the army. Just to illustrate that, sir, in 1992, in the month of February - and I have that document which says that the Serbian Democratic Party distributed 17.000 pieces of weaponry to the Serbian people and the JNA distributed 56.000 pieces of infantry weapons to the Serbian people. I have that document. I've not got it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What time are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992. Perhaps January, February of that year. I have that official document. It exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that document. You had a lengthy discussion about that document with Mr. Ackerman, a document, and I'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Can you show it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Is it correct paramilitary formations were also set up in the territory which is currently the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and were people armed there? Which paramilitary formations were set up by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I know that they were organised also in that area, and those units were called units for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina because the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up for the entire Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they clashed with the army -- Serbian army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Departments were set up in municipalities as well as companies and squads. Those formations were being set up in order to defend the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those units were set up in 1991; right? And they were known as the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and so on and so forth. Would you agree with me that they were not organised in order to fight the VRS but the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. On the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1991, we had a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina. 64 per cent of the population were in favour of the independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The European community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to legality, do you know, according to the then-valid constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina what percentage would have made referendum legal? How much did you study the constitutional law at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I did not study it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will not go that way. I'm not asking you that. Please look at me and answer my questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, take a pause between question and answer. Mr. Selak, you're not here to debate with Mr. Lukic. You're here to answer his questions. If something very important might have been missing, you'll have an opportunity or the Prosecution will ask you further questions about that. Please focus your answers on what Mr. Lukic asks you and not what you think he should have asked for. He is putting the questions to you. You give the answers. Could you please abide by that. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you familiar with the fact that units were organised under the name of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the exact date. However, towards the end of 1991 I believe that they existed because they were being prepared for the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, the only legitimate armed force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was legitimate then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: When Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared as an independent state, the JNA had to withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hold on. Did the JNA withdraw -- withdrew in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's get things calmed down. In your first answer, Mr. Selak, you already did not what I asked you to do. You were asked whether you're familiar with the fact that units were organised under certain names. Apparently, I do understand from your answer, that you were aware but you started adding what their job was. You were not asked about that. Then in one of the answers which followed, you said: "When Bosnia-Herzegovina was declared as an independent state, the JNA had to withdraw." What we'd like to know is, if you refer to such a point in time, that you give us that point in time. Apart from that, Mr. Lukic, I invited Mr. Selak not to consider your exchange as a conversation or a debate but as questions and answers, and then preferably about facts. Legitimate forces, et cetera, and that is known in this Tribunal, have raised eternal discussions on what was legitimate or not. And, finally, that is a legal matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have not completed my answer. Your Honours, the JNA did not withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The only exception being the conscripts who were serving their compulsory army service and who hailed from Serbia or Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked whether the JNA withdrew in 1991. Your answer was no, they didn't. So you had answered that question. And if Mr. Lukic wants to know any further details, then he'll ask for it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know what the numerical strength of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which political parties advocated and instructed the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to respond to the JNA call-ups?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: There were many parties. I can't give you their names. I can't answer your question because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, is there a dispute about the positions of the political parties in relation to the JNA call-ups?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No dispute Your Honour. And the Prosecution is always welcome to consider any facts that the Defence might propose that we would agree to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can challenge credibility of the witness by this, because on the transcript, page 13214, from 2nd January 2003, he explicitly stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, then you should at least -- if you want the Chamber to understand this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then I think you should provide the Chamber with the relevant information. 2003, transcript page. That's in another case. You refer to another -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Is that in evidence at this moment for us if you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Please proceed. Then at this moment -- Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You answered a question by saying Alija Izetbegovic suggested that Bosniaks should not respond to such call-ups. And you said that you were familiar with that statement. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I can't remember the words. It was only -- it was some nine or ten years ago. Politics are politics. I'm sure that Alija Izetbegovic did advocate that political options and solutions, but I can't remember the data -- the details. I'm getting on, you know, so I can't answer in the affirmative. I believe that something like that was done but -- and I signed that, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't sign anything. You said it under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Do you know or do you not know whether Mr. Izetbegovic and his political party were in favour of following the call-ups or that they advised persons not to respond to such call-ups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, Your Honours. Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been divided. There were areas with the executive power of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that there were call-ups for that area. But he didn't have any influence on the mobilisation in the territory of the VRS. He could not influence that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1991?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 1991 there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about 1992. Mr. Lukic has not limited his questions, and even reference was made earlier to 1991, I think. What was the position, to your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the position of Mr. Izetbegovic and his party, whether you should respond positively to call-ups for the JNA even before the Republika Srpska did exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure. I did not receive any official information from politicians. I was subordinated to the command of the JNA. We did not receive that kind of information or at least not us in Banja Luka. I did not listen to Radio Sarajevo which broadcast such information. I'm sure that such things existed, that there was a lot of propaganda going on, but I never heard any such propaganda messages, so I cannot answer in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say you did not receive any official information. As a matter of fact, you explained that you had no information at all. Nevertheless, your answer to the question in 2003, if rightly quoted by Mr. Lukic, suggests that you knew the position of Mr. Izetbegovic by whatever sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with Izetbegovic's position. He wanted a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina and that is a fact, Your Honours. I was aware of that and I was in favour of that myself. He wanted that republic to be a -- set up of all the three constituent peoples, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, i.e., the Bosniaks, and he advocated that option all the time, until the day he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is not focussing on the call-ups as you were asked to do. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this a good time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a good time for a break as well. We take a break and resume at a quarter to 2.00. But, first, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, listen carefully to the questions that Mr. Lukic will put to you and answer them as briefly as possible. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, we have kept raising new issues. You mentioned Mr. Izetbegovic and you said that he was in favour of a united Bosnia-Herzegovina and that he fought for that concept until the very end of his life. Is it also true that he also fought for a Bosnia-Herzegovina outside of Yugoslavia and without the JNA?

I know that he participated in the negotiations when Yugoslavia was breaking apart, unfortunately. I was a member of that Yugoslav People's Army as a Yugoslav. However, politics are politics. I didn't want to get involved, I don't know any details, and I don't want to answer your question by saying something that I'm not positive about and I don't have accurate information about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 4th of April, 1992, Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?
I'm not sure of the date, but I know that a state of war was indeed proclaimed, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was that aimed against, in your view?
In my view, against all those who were against Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state of all of its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that means against 99 per cent of the Serbs?

The Serbian Democratic Party, sir, officially proclaimed Republika Srpska. I have documents in which it says that they wanted to be united with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Alija Izetbegovic was against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that Alija Izetbegovic proclaimed a state of war and thus proclaimed that he would start waging a war against the Serbian people in Yugoslavia?
That was also done by Mr. Karadzic. I have that document as well. He also proclaimed a state of war in his turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that a state of war in Republika Srpska was proclaimed only in the second half of 1995?
I am not aware of the date, but I know that it was, indeed, proclaimed. I'm not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think it would be in the interest of the work of this Chamber to -- that you focus primarily on matters of factual knowledge of this witness. And the last series of questions have demonstrated, to some extent I would say, and it might be that you want to establish that, that this witness has his own firm political opinions on certain matters. And if that's what you want to emphasise, then that message has been received. And Judge Moloto may want to put a question or two. Give any comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are at page 83, line 6, as saying in the second half of 1995. Did you want to say 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, for SDS, for Republika Srpska. Time of war was declared only in 1995, second part, and only on a part of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. And again, focus on factual knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rather than being at risk to enter into a debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be provided with a statement. I can't provide him with mine because I've underlined things in it. Maybe the Prosecutor can provide his statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I brought a clean copy to court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You do recognise your statement, don't you?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's advance to paragraph 44, please. You say at the beginning: "The other officers told me that Talic usually attended the meetings of the regional Crisis Staff." My question is this: You yourself never attended any of those meetings with General Talic; right?
No. I wasn't. But his officers stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who told you that?
My colleagues. I can't tell you exactly who -- please. The corps command was the corps command, the bases [as interpreted] had its office one floor above him. That was our regular communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the name and the family name of the person who told you or not?
I can't. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on.

Your Honours, when I asked for General Talic, several times I was told that he was at a meeting of the Crisis Staff. This was from the corps command, information from the corps command, so I don't know who told me about that. Ten years have passed since then. Over ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to justify that you don't know anymore. Just listen carefully to the questions, answer them, tell us what you know, tell us what you do not know anymore. And, Mr. Lukic, calmness would certainly assist in obtaining the best evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, was there a republican Crisis Staff?
No. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.
Only in the regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 45, it's at the beginning of the paragraph, it says: "I know that from the end of 1991 training was provided for paramilitary formations in Manjaca. Paramilitary formations can be considered to be all men who are armed but are not part of the army or the MUP." At the time in 1991, the end of 1991, were there still Territorial Defence units in existence?

The Territorial Defence units were disbanded in 1991, as early of 1991, throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The weapons were supposed to be returned to the warehouses, but this was not all completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when these Territorial Defence units were disbanded, approximately, in 1991?
It was at the beginning of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The army never issued orders of any kind to the paramilitary units. That's what you stated in the Tadic case. Do you stand by that today?

It didn't issue them with any orders, but later in the documents even the Chief of the Main Staff said that volunteer units should be established as soon as possible and they should be armed and even that JNA officers should become part of such units. I have such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is the chief and of which Main Staff?
Of the JNA, the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade?
Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, if you want to consult, do it at a low voice and not from a distance with a loud voice. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at paragraph 48 where you speak about to whom you were subordinated, about the structure you were a part of.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say: "As a commander of the logistics base, I wasn't subordinated to General Uzelac but to the command of the 1st Army in Belgrade." Were you subordinated to the 1st Army, to the 5th Army, to the 2nd Army, or to the SSNO?

No. I was subordinated to the 1st Army District in Belgrade. And, later, when the 2nd Military District was established in Sarajevo, I was subordinated to that district. Never to the 5th. The bases were under the direct command of the army, not of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll move on, as I'm not really an expert when it comes to your channels of commanding and reporting. Isn't it true that your area, the 5th Corps and that area, was under the 5th Military District?
No, that was never the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 5th Corps, the 5th Banja Luka Corps wasn't part of the 5th Army?
No, it was part of the 7th Army District and later of the 2nd one. It was never part of the 5th Military District. That district was in Zagreb, so it was never under its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. So were you subordinated to the 1st Military District or the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

The bases were all under the command of the Military Districts. For one period of time I was under the command of the 1st Military Command, and then under the 2nd Military Command when it was established in Sarajevo under the command of General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will move onto paragraph 53 now. You say: "In the middle of July 1992 Talic requested a meeting with me in order to inform me that I was not allowed to leave Banja Luka." We can't ask General Talic about this, but I would like you to tell me who was present at that conversation?
I think it was Colonel Ninkovic. I think it was Colonel Ninkovic. Don't hold me to that, though. But I think that was the case. He is in Banja Luka now. You can contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you leave Banja Luka in spite of this?
Yes. In 1995 when my wife fell ill, I asked General Mladic to allow me to leave and to go to Belgrade to the Military Medical Academy in an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this made possible for you?

I phoned General Djukic, he put me through to General Mladic, and he said that he ordered Colonel Marjanovic to take me to Belgrade. Colonel Marjanovic didn't want to take me there, so I paid two Serbs from Banja Luka 2.800 German marks to take me to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You stayed there for 13 days; is that correct?
Yes, for about 12 or 13 days, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- Mr. Lukic, could you take care that consultations in the back are not disturbing the continuation of the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that 13-day period, Mr. Selak?
I went to see my son in Wiesbaden, in Germany. He is a doctor and he operated on his mother there. Unfortunately, she later died.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now have a look at paragraph 55. In this paragraph, you say: "In the middle of July 1992, I was elected to be the commander of the resistance staff in Banja Luka." You were referring to resistance to the Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

The resistance staff in Banja Luka to resist the organs in power and those who maltreated Muslims and Croats, because they were fleeing Banja Luka en masse. And it's true that we established this body not as against Republika Srpska as such but against the events happening in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were the people with you in that group?
I can't answer that question for the sake of their safety. Your Honours, please allow me not to mention the names of these people. It is for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there anyone who does not live --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For -- first of all, I think there's no need to stand, for Mr. Mladic. Now, you'd like not to mention those names, not in public, at least. Would you mind to mention the names in private session? Which means that those persons would -- that -- the names you are telling us are not broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to say that this resistance movement - I have to explain this - didn't amount to resistance of any kind because we assessed the situation and the corps had 100.000 people and we had between 500 and 1.000 men who were not armed, so we did not -- and I can't mention any names because of their safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, my question was whether you would be willing to give the names in private session. Are you willing to do so? That means that those participating in these proceedings --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll have to consult with my -- Mr. Groome, you would like to make any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe before the Chamber deliberates on this, I think it might be helped by knowing what is the relevance of this. I have a hard time understanding what the relevance is at this stage. Perhaps there is idea of relevance, but I would appreciate knowing what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps before we further consider the matter, Mr. Lukic, could you explain what the relevance is to know those -- these names?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is self-explanatory, Your Honour. The whole statement is full of explanations how there was mistrust on the Serbian side toward this gentleman and Muslims in general and now we can get a base for that, that mistrust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By receiving those names?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would be able to further investigate what was it, when it was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure the legal requirement of a question being relevant is that it would enable further investigations. I believe that would be a matter for Defence investigators to do and to make some inquiry in the Banja Luka area. I think what needs to be demonstrated at this point is why is it relevant to the determination that this Chamber has to make when adjudicating this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the witness will have to answer that question is something we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the Chamber will insist on the witness answering the question, we'll discuss that and let you know, if possible, this afternoon. At least not any later than tomorrow morning. We would like to pay proper attention to it. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Lukic. I have one or two small procedural items which I would like to briefly deal with. Therefore, I suggest that we adjourn for the day after I have dealt with those and that the witness is already excused at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Selak -- yes, Mr. Groome. Any?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has to do with the scheduling for the witness, Your Honour. Tomorrow there is a videolink scheduled and Mr. Lukic informs that he thinks that he will take the entire day for the cross-examination. Can I ask that Mr. Selak be allowed to remain on standby in his hotel room? I think, if needed, we can get him here in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Selak, we'll resume your examination either tomorrow, but not right away at 9.30 in the morning, or perhaps even the day after tomorrow. Therefore, as Mr. Groome asked, you do not have to come to the Tribunal in the morning but you should remain standby so as to be able to start immediately once we have dealt with another witness who will give his testimony through videolink. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I also would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given. If you have understood this message, then you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two brief matters. First, and I'm primarily addressing the Defence, on the 22nd and the 23rd of August, the Defence objected to the admission of MFIs P80 and P89, which had been tendered by the Prosecution as associated exhibits through 92 ter Witness van Lynden. The Defence submitted in court that it would make written submissions in relation to these MFIs. That can be found on transcript pages 1472 to 1473 and 1477 to 1479. On the 21st of September, the Defence informed the Chamber through an informal communication that it no longer intended to submit a filing in relation to the aforementioned MFIs. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber understands the Defence objections to MFIs P80 and P89 to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, therefore, P80 and P89 are admitted into evidence. One last matter, I'm addressing you, Mr. Groome. The Chamber suggests to you that you already number the paragraphs of witness statements when you attach them to your 92 ter motions, and not only at a later stage because we might work on hard copies of it, make our notes on it, and then have to number them at a later stage ourselves. I think it would be best to just briefly mention that in half a sentence in a 92 ter motion so that we always know whether the numbering of the paragraphs has been added at that moment in time or whether the paragraphs were already numbered at an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We'll do that from this point forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 26th of September, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
